sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in Kelowna
sections.html:
Kelowna gets about 3,715 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −16.1°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Kelowna. That's about 6% less heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover.

Of Kelowna's 41,965 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 50% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

• Combustion safety. In the Kelowna area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 63% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in Kelowna
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 17.4% of 109 homes tested in the Okanagan Health Service Delivery Area health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 28.5% (1 in 3) of houses at or above the guideline for the Kelowna, BC (Kelowna CMA) metro area. Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. There's no provincial price list; the City of Nanaimo quotes $400–$500 as typical for an existing home. Several B.C. municipalities subsidize evaluations for their residents (see local programs below).

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Kelowna: CSA F280-12 heat pump sizing for −16.1°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280-12 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Kelowna homes, sized to the local −16.1°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −16.1°C for Kelowna, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Kelowna.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Kelowna
sections.html:
−16.1°C is the 20th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −16.1°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Kelowna area, 72% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace; natural gas is the main heating energy for 63% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023).

The National Building Code 2020 requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. Provincial codes can name their own edition and climate values, so ask your designer which ones the calculation uses.

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Kelowna
radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Kelowna: long-term monitoring, kits and mitigation
radon-testing.description: Radon in Kelowna: Health Canada survey results for the Okanagan Health Service Delivery Area region (17.4% above the guideline), how to run a 91-day long-term test, digital monitors versus alpha-track kits, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals ($2,000–$3,000).
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 17.4% of homes tested in the Okanagan Health Service Delivery Area health region were above the guideline, and only a long-term test tells you about your own house.

glance.sub: the Kelowna, BC (Kelowna CMA) metro area

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 17.4% of 109 homes tested in the Okanagan Health Service Delivery Area health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 28.5% (1 in 3) of houses at or above the guideline for the Kelowna, BC (Kelowna CMA) metro area.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months. Our radon testing guide walks through each step.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. The choice of device:

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends. A long-term kit costs about $30–$80 including the lab fee (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit).
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app, and cost more (Lung Saskatchewan sells one for $189). For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.
  • Continuous monitoring after mitigation: a digital monitor left running lets you watch for changes between the follow-up long-term tests Health Canada recommends.

• BC Lung's library lending program puts radon detectors in many BC libraries, free with a library card, and the BC Centre for Disease Control publishes a BC Radon Map of results by area.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Kelowna postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP. After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

sections.h2: Rules and help in British Columbia
sections.html:
• Since March 2024, the BC Building Code requires a radon rough-in in all new houses province-wide.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Kelowna?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 17.4% of 109 homes tested in the Okanagan Health Service Delivery Area health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 28.5% (1 in 3) of houses at or above the guideline for the Kelowna, BC (Kelowna CMA) metro area. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least 91 days, in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Kelowna?
faq.a: BC Lung's library lending program puts radon detectors in many BC libraries, free with a library card, and the BC Centre for Disease Control publishes a BC Radon Map of results by area. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits, for about $30–$80 including the lab fee.

faq.q: Digital radon monitor or alpha-track kit?
faq.a: An alpha-track kit is the cheaper long-term test: it sits for three months or more and goes to a lab. A digital monitor shows readings as it goes and can keep running after mitigation; for a long-term result, use one that has passed C-NRPP testing and run it for at least three months.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan. Hire a C-NRPP-certified mitigation professional.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test in the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Kelowna: air sampling, inspection and remediation
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Kelowna: when mold sampling is worth it, why cold winters cause condensation, the CMHC and Health Canada size rules for cleanup, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: Mould sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mould problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure. Here's how to inspect a home in Kelowna, when air quality testing helps, and how much cleanup you can safely do yourself.

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Kelowna homes
sections.html:
Kelowna gets about 3,715 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −16.1°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Kelowna. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mould usually starts in Kelowna houses.

Of Kelowna's 41,965 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 50% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling is worth it
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Air or surface sampling helps in three cases:

  • You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester, lab or remediation contractor
sections.html:
Ask any Kelowna tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned.

faq.q: How much does mould testing cost in Kelowna?
faq.a: We found no reputable Canadian source for the cost of a professional mould assessment, so get two or three written quotes and ask how many samples are included, which lab analyzes them and what the report covers.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.h1: Asbestos testing and inspection in Kelowna
asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing and inspection in Kelowna: vermiculite, labs, and British Columbia abatement and removal rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos inspection and testing in Kelowna, where 50% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs, the British Columbia rules for renovation, and what abatement and removal involve if a test is positive.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 21,100 Kelowna houses (50%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Kelowna houses
sections.html:
Of Kelowna's 41,965 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 50% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

B.C. has Canada's strictest regime: before renovation or demolition work, a qualified person must inspect and sample for hazardous materials such as asbestos and lead (OHS Regulation s. 20.112), and since January 1, 2024, asbestos abatement contractors must be licensed by WorkSafeBC.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

sections.h2: If it's positive: abatement and removal
sections.html:
Leave the material alone until a plan is in place. For vermiculite, Health Canada says not to use the attic for storage, to keep children out and to seal gaps around the attic hatch, light fixtures and outlets, and to hire professionals trained to handle asbestos if you plan to renovate.

In British Columbia: Since January 1, 2024, asbestos abatement contractors must be licensed by WorkSafeBC, which publishes a registry of licensed contractors, and anyone doing abatement work needs mandatory training and a certificate. Hazardous materials found in the pre-renovation inspection must be safely contained or removed.

Abatement is quoted separately from testing. Get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the waste will be disposed of.

faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Kelowna: at-risk homes, testing and safe abatement
lead-paint-testing.description: 8% of Kelowna's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 8% of Kelowna's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 42% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which Kelowna homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Kelowna's 41,965 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 50% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive: lead paint abatement
sections.html:
Health Canada says leaving lead-based paint alone is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach, and covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling adds protection. Paint that's chipping, flaking or within reach of children is a serious hazard and has to come off carefully; consider hiring an expert before you start.

No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. must include lead in pre-renovation and demolition hazard inspections, and in Yukon before demolition. If you do the work yourself, Health Canada's precautions are:

  • Don't use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps: they create toxic dust and fumes. For do-it-yourself work, Health Canada suggests a chemical paint-stripper paste applied with a brush.
  • Move furniture out or cover it with plastic, seal doorways and vents with plastic sheeting and tape, and run a fan blowing out through an open window.
  • Wear goggles, gloves and a good-quality mask, work in 10-minute stretches with breaks outdoors, and don't eat, drink or smoke in the work area.
  • Clean up daily: put scrapings in a sealed container marked Hazardous Waste, follow your municipality's disposal instructions, and wipe surfaces with a damp cloth you throw away.
  • Keep children and pregnant people away until the work is done; Health Canada says there is no known safe level of lead exposure.

faq.q: Does my Kelowna house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

faq.q: Should I remove lead paint or cover it?
faq.a: Health Canada says leaving it alone or covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach. Never sand it or use a heat gun, and consider hiring an expert for removal.

well-water-testing.lede: Kelowna is served by the City's water utility and several independent water districts, and it also includes rural and agricultural land. If yours is, here's how testing works in British Columbia.

sections.html: Kelowna is served by the City's water utility and several independent water districts, and it also includes rural and agricultural land.

sections.h2: How testing works in British Columbia
sections.html: There's no free provincial program: use a qualified lab (search the CALA directory), which supplies the bottles. HealthLinkBC recommends testing for bacteria at least once a year and for chemistry when the well is new and annually after that.

• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: For bacteria, at least once a year and after flooding, heavy rain or well work; many health units recommend more often. Test chemistry when the well is new and every few years after.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Kelowna: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Kelowna: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 5 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Kelowna: no mandatory reporting rule and 5 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Kelowna
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.BC).

• Continuous Optimization (C-Op) program (BC Hydro in partnership with FortisBC): Funding of up to $0.15 per sq ft for an approved service provider to retro-commission or recommission HVAC and other systems; 75% is paid after the investigation stage and 25% on completion. Details
  • Commercial Energy Assessment Program (FortisBC): Free walkthrough energy assessment by a FortisBC-authorized consultant, with a report within 60 days listing low/no-cost measures, possible upgrades and applicable FortisBC rebates. Details
  • Custom Efficiency Program - energy study funding (FortisBC): Up to 50% of an energy study by a FortisBC-approved consultant (max $20,000 for commercial buildings), plus an implementation bonus of up to another 50% of the study cost (max $20,000) once approved measures are installed. Implementation incentives: the lesser of $6/GJ (gas) or $0.03/kWh (electric) over measure life, 75% of invoiced costs, or $500,000 for commercial buildings. Details
  • Energy efficiency for rental apartments and accommodations program (FortisBC): Free building energy assessment by FortisBC engineering consultants plus free in-suite showerheads, aerators, pipe insulation and hot-water recirculation controls, with ongoing support for larger upgrades. Details
  • Energy-saving support for small businesses program (FortisBC with GreenStep Solutions): Free customized energy advice (15-30 minute consultation by phone, video or in person), which may include a basic energy assessment and rebate information, with a follow-up email. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Kelowna buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: We found no mandatory reporting rule for Kelowna buildings as of September 28, 2026.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Kelowna?
faq.a: Yes: Continuous Optimization (C-Op) program; Commercial Energy Assessment Program; Custom Efficiency Program - energy study funding; Energy efficiency for rental apartments and accommodations program. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
